analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from referring patients to labs, imaging centers, and equipment suppliers they own or get paid by.
analysis.headline: Referred to committee on the day it was introduced, the bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred doctors from sending patients for lab tests, imaging, physical therapy, medical equipment, home health, and other services to businesses in which the doctor or a family member had an ownership stake or payment arrangement. Today, a doctor who co-owns a testing lab has a financial reason to order more tests; this bill would have cut off that incentive, with civil fines for doctors and companies that billed around the rule. It sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, and everyone who pays the bills — Medicare, insurers, employers, and families — would benefit from fewer tests ordered for the doctor's profit rather than the patient's need. Doctors who do not own testing facilities would also face fairer competition from colleagues who currently profit from their own referrals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and everyone who pays health bills

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a physician from referring patients for designated health services — clinical lab tests, imaging, physical and occupational therapy, radiation therapy, medical equipment, home health, outpatient drugs, and hospital services — to an entity in which the physician or an immediate family member has an ownership or investment interest or a compensation arrangement.
Bars entities from billing patients or insurers for services furnished under a prohibited referral, and requires refunds of any amounts collected in violation.
Sets civil money penalties of up to $15,000 per improper claim, up to $100,000 for deliberately structured referral schemes, and up to $10,000 per day for failing to report ownership arrangements.
Requires health service entities to report to the government which physicians own them, exposing referral-driven ownership arrangements to scrutiny.

analysis.who_pays: Physicians who invested in labs, imaging centers, physical therapy clinics, and equipment supply businesses would lose the ability to profit from their own referrals. All physicians and health entities would bear paperwork costs of reporting and compliance, and some patients might face somewhat less convenient access to in-office services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Physician investors in medical service businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out a large exception for 'in-office ancillary services' and same-group-practice referrals, meaning physicians in group practices could keep referring patients to services their own group owns and bills for — the very incentive the bill targets elsewhere.

It exempts ownership of publicly traded securities in large corporations (over $75 million in stockholder equity) and allows doctors to keep hospital ownership stakes if they have staff privileges, steering referral profits toward large corporate and hospital-based providers rather than eliminating them.

Physicians would face significant compliance and reporting obligations, and the 'fair market value' tests for leases, employment, and recruitment arrangements would invite disputes and regulatory paperwork.
The bill includes rural and Puerto Rico exceptions out of concern that banning physician ownership could reduce access to services in areas with few providers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the financial incentive for doctors to order services they profit from — directly addresses overuse and excess billing that patients, Medicare, and insurers pay for. But the design has real weaknesses: the in-office and group-practice exceptions preserve much of the self-referral incentive, and the exemption for publicly traded large corporations shifts advantages to big corporate providers. On balance a meaningful patient protection, though an imperfect one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to its health subcommittee five weeks later, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman, joined by Mr. Stark, introduced the bill in the House on September 9, 1993.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, September 9, 1993.
On October 5, 1993, it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where the record shows no further action.
No committee vote, floor vote, or companion Senate action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians and investors who own clinical labs, imaging centers, therapy clinics, and medical equipment businesses kept the ability to profit from referring their own patients to those facilities. No one else gained from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Physician owners of labs and imaging centers

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Physician Ownership and Referral Act of 1993 in the House on September 9, 1993.

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.role: Cosponsor; senior Democrat on the House Ways and Means health subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman in introducing the bill, which limits physician referrals for financial gain.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 9, 1993, and never reported it out; it was instead sent to a subcommittee and never advanced to a vote.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a committee vote or to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split can be measured; the bill's two named supporters were Democrats, and the committee that held it was run by Democrats as well.

industries.industry: Physician-owned labs, imaging centers, therapy clinics, and medical equipment suppliers
industries.note: These businesses exist because referring physicians own them or are paid by them, and the bill would ban billing for self-referred lab work, imaging, therapy, and equipment. Their revenue comes from tests and services ordered partly for the owner's profit, a cost borne by patients and insurers.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded health service companies
industries.note: The bill exempts physician ownership of publicly traded stock in companies with over $75 million in stockholder equity, so corporate lab and imaging chains would lose physician-owned competitors while remaining permissible vehicles for physician investment.

The bill lets doctors keep ownership stakes in hospitals where they have staff privileges and exempts Puerto Rico hospitals and physician recruitment payments, so hospital-based referral arrangements largely continue, while hospitals would face reporting and penalty rules.
